# Module 2. The Great Hall: dashboard model notes

This is everything I need to build the Power BI dashboard: the star schema, the
relationships, the DAX for every measure, and the six pages with the finding
each one carries.

**The Power BI project is generated by a script.** Run
[`src/analysis/29_build_powerbi_project.py`](../src/analysis/29_build_powerbi_project.py)
and it writes [`pbip/DataWizardry.pbip`](pbip/). This is a Power BI project in
Microsoft's open `.pbip` format. It holds the eleven tables, the eight
relationships and all twenty measures. Power BI Desktop opens it directly,
and **File, Save As** makes the `.pbix`.

A script cannot make a `.pbix`. It is a ZIP around a compiled Analysis Services
model, and only Power BI Desktop can produce that. `.pbip` is the text format
that gets around the problem.

**I confirmed that it opens.** The project loads in Power BI Desktop 2.150
(25.12) with all eleven tables, the twenty measures on `Key Measures`, and the
six named pages. It took one round trip to get there. My first version named the
measures table `Measures`. Power BI reserves that name, so it rejected the whole
file with "Unsupported Table name". I fixed that. The generator now refuses to
write any reserved name, and `tests/test_powerbi_project.py` fails if one
appears.

The generator still cannot open its own output, because a script cannot drive a
GUI application. It checks that the JSON is well formed, that the relationships
point at columns which really exist, and that the M queries point at files which
are really on disk. It checks nothing more. Anything beyond that I can only find
by opening the project.

### Applying the palette

The report comes with Power BI's default colours. To match the figures, the
infographic and the web page, import the theme once:

**View, Themes, Browse for themes**, then pick `dashboard/DataWizardryTheme.json`

It sets dark turquoise as the main series colour, deep blue as the second, gold
for callouts, and the text styles. The same values are in
`src/utils/plotting.py` and `web/css/base.css`. All three must change together,
or the three deliverables stop looking like one piece of work.

I keep the theme as a separate file and do not embed it in the project.
Embedding it means editing the report's resource packages. I cannot test that
with a script, and a badly formed theme resource stops the whole report from
opening. Saving one click on the import is not worth that risk.

### Opening it

1. Open `pbip/DataWizardry.pbip` in Power BI Desktop.
2. On first open it warns that relationships need refreshing and that tables have
   no data. This is expected and it is not a fault. A project defines the model
   but stores no rows, so nothing has been read yet. Click **Refresh now**. This
   runs the M queries against `dashboard/model/*.csv`.
3. **File, Save As** makes the `.pbix`.

The script also lays out the six pages. It places 30 visuals: 9 on Overview, 4
on Return on investment, 4 on Reception, 3 on Geography, 6 on Product line and 4
on Timing. A script cannot open the report, so my tests only check that every
page has visuals, that every visual uses fields that exist in the model, and
that every visual stays on the canvas. How the pages really look I can only see
by opening the project.

The M queries use absolute paths, so if I move the repository I have to run the
generator again.

## The star schema

Five dimensions and five facts. There are ten files in [`model/`](model/). They
are made again from `data/processed` each time I rerun the analysis.

```
                    ┌─────────────┐
                    │  dim_date   │  456 rows, grain: month
                    └──────┬──────┘
                           │ date_key
     ┌──────────────┬──────┴───────┬──────────────┬─────────────────┐
     │              │              │              │                 │
┌────┴─────┐  ┌─────┴──────┐  ┌────┴─────┐  ┌─────┴──────┐  ┌───────┴────────┐
│fact_film │  │fact_atten- │  │fact_ret- │  │fact_prod-  │  │fact_park_      │
│_perform- │  │tion_month- │  │ail_month-│  │uct_release │  │attendance      │
│ance   11 │  │ly    9,624 │  │ly  9,015 │  │       265  │  │           66   │
└────┬─────┘  └─────┬──────┘  └──────────┘  └─────┬──────┘  └────────────────┘
     │ film_key     │ series                      │ theme_key
┌────┴─────┐  ┌─────┴─────────┐            ┌──────┴──────────┐
│ dim_film │  │ dim_character │            │dim_product_theme│
│    11    │  │      16       │            │       5         │
└──────────┘  └───────────────┘            └─────────────────┘

dim_country (61 rows) is unrelated in the model and filters the
```

### Relationships to create

The same list, in a form a script can read, is in
[`model/relationships.csv`](model/relationships.csv).

| From | Column | To | Column | Cardinality | Cross filter |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| dim_date | date_key | fact_film_performance | date_key | 1:* | single |
| dim_date | date_key | fact_attention_monthly | date_key | 1:* | single |
| dim_date | date_key | fact_retail_monthly | date_key | 1:* | single |
| dim_date | date_key | fact_product_release | date_key | 1:* | single |
| dim_date | date_key | fact_park_attendance | date_key | 1:* | single |
| dim_film | film_key | fact_film_performance | film_key | 1:1 | both |
| dim_product_theme | theme_key | fact_product_release | theme_key | 1:* | single |
| dim_character | article | fact_attention_monthly | series | 1:* | single |

### Three modelling decisions worth defending

**One grain per fact table, and everything monthly.** The attention data is
weekly by nature. I roll it up to monthly before it goes into the model.
Publishing both a weekly and a monthly attention fact against one date dimension
is the usual way a star schema quietly counts things twice. So only one grain
exists.

**`dim_character` joins on `article`, not on a surrogate key.** The character
dimension only holds the sixteen main cast members that have a mapped Wikipedia
article. `article` is the only column that appears on both sides. A surrogate
key would add a lookup step and no new information at this size. The join is one
to many because `fact_attention_monthly` also holds franchise, film and control
series that no character matches. Those rows just have no character context, and
that is correct.

**`dim_country` is unrelated on purpose.** The regional search interest data is
a single snapshot across countries for each keyword group. It is not a time
series. So it has no `date_key`, and it cannot join the rest of the model unless
I invent one. It feeds the Geography page directly. Relating it would create an
ambiguous path, and a filter that looks like it works but means nothing.

## DAX measures

My plan named five measures. All five are here, plus the supporting ones the
pages need. Paste them into a single measure table.

The project file holds twenty measures. Seventeen of them are written out below.
The other three are simple and are only in the project file: `Set Count`,
`Film Count` and `Critic Audience Gap`. One measure below, `Average Price Per
Piece Real`, is not in the project file yet, because it has no price data to
read.

### Film performance

```dax
Total Budget =
SUM ( fact_film_performance[budget_usd] )
```

```dax
Total Worldwide Gross =
SUM ( fact_film_performance[worldwide_gross_usd] )
```

```dax
Profit =
[Total Worldwide Gross] - [Total Budget]
```

```dax
Profit Margin =
DIVIDE ( [Profit], [Total Worldwide Gross] )
```

```dax
Return on Budget =
DIVIDE ( [Total Worldwide Gross], [Total Budget] )
```

`Profit` here does not take off marketing spend or the exhibitor's share, so it
is higher than true profit. Label it "gross profit" on every visual.

### Cumulative franchise revenue

```dax
Cumulative Franchise Revenue =
CALCULATE (
    [Total Worldwide Gross],
    FILTER (
        ALLSELECTED ( dim_date[date_key] ),
        dim_date[date_key] <= MAX ( dim_date[date_key] )
    )
)
```

I use `ALLSELECTED` and not `ALL` so the running total respects the era slicer
and does not ignore it. A reader who filters to one era expects the total to
follow the filter.

### Attention

```dax
Mean Weekly Attention =
AVERAGE ( fact_attention_monthly[mean_weekly_value] )
```

```dax
Attention YoY Change =
VAR CurrentValue = [Mean Weekly Attention]
VAR PriorValue =
    CALCULATE (
        [Mean Weekly Attention],
        DATEADD ( dim_date[month_start], -12, MONTH )
    )
RETURN
    DIVIDE ( CurrentValue - PriorValue, PriorValue )
```

```dax
Franchise Attention =
CALCULATE (
    [Mean Weekly Attention],
    fact_attention_monthly[source] = "wikipedia_pageviews",
    fact_attention_monthly[group] = "franchise"
)
```

### Retail and seasonality

```dax
Category Sales Real =
CALCULATE (
    SUM ( fact_retail_monthly[sales_thousands_cad_real] ),
    fact_retail_monthly[is_focus_category] = TRUE ()
)
```

```dax
Total Retail Sales Real =
CALCULATE (
    SUM ( fact_retail_monthly[sales_thousands_cad_real] ),
    fact_retail_monthly[is_total_retail] = TRUE ()
)
```

```dax
Seasonality Index =
VAR MonthlyValue = [Category Sales Real]
VAR AnnualAverage =
    CALCULATE (
        AVERAGEX ( VALUES ( dim_date[date_key] ), [Category Sales Real] ),
        ALLEXCEPT ( dim_date, dim_date[year] )
    )
RETURN
    DIVIDE ( MonthlyValue, AnnualAverage ) * 100
```

100 is an average month for that year. December reads about 172 on the focus
category. That is the number my whole timing argument rests on.

```dax
Category Share of Total Retail =
DIVIDE ( [Category Sales Real], [Total Retail Sales Real] )
```

### Product pricing

```dax
Total Pieces =
SUM ( fact_product_release[num_parts] )
```

```dax
Average Price Per Piece =
AVERAGE ( fact_product_release[price_per_piece_cad] )
```

```dax
Average Price Per Piece Real =
AVERAGE ( fact_product_release[price_per_piece_cad_real] )
```

Both price measures return blank until I have a Brickset API key and
`07_brickset.py` has run. That is the correct behaviour and the measure is not
broken. The Product line page should show a clear "price source not collected"
note and not a zero, because zero is a price and blank means nothing was
collected.

### Park attendance

```dax
Total Attendance =
SUM ( fact_park_attendance[attendance] )
```

```dax
Attendance Index vs Pre-Opening =
AVERAGE ( fact_park_attendance[attendance_index_vs_year_before_opening] )
```

## The six pages

I want every page to have a one line title that states a finding, not a label.
The titles below are the findings my analysis really produced. Where a page's
finding depends on data I did not collect, I say so and I do not hide it.

### 1. Overview

**Title:** "Franchise attention has fallen 57 per cent since its 2023 peak, while
the new series' own article has risen a hundredfold."

Both halves are measured. The composite of the four franchise articles averaged
282,101 weekly views in 2023 and 121,570 in 2026. The show's own article went
from about 40 views a day through 2024 to roughly 5,000 from the middle of 2025.
The old franchise and the new series are moving in opposite directions. This is
the most important thing a category buyer needs to understand about 2026.

A line chart of `Franchise Attention` by month across the full window, with
`Cumulative Franchise Revenue` on a second axis. Cards for total franchise
revenue, film count and the current attention level. The headline finding from
[`../docs/findings.md`](../docs/findings.md) goes in a text box on the page, not
in a tooltip.

### 2. Return on investment

**Title:** "Deathly Hallows Part 2 returned 10.5 times its assigned budget; The
Secrets of Dumbledore returned 2.0, and every Fantastic Beasts film did worse
than every Harry Potter film."

A scatter of `Total Budget` against `Total Worldwide Gross`, one point per film,
with bubble size `Profit` and colour by `dim_film[era]`. Add a note on the page
that the Deathly Hallows budget split is a convention and not a measurement,
because it makes Part 2 look better.

### 3. Reception

**Title:** "Audiences rated The Secrets of Dumbledore 37 points above critics;
Goblet of Fire is the only film critics liked markedly more than audiences."

The three largest gaps are Secrets of Dumbledore at -37, Crimes of Grindelwald at
-17 and Goblet of Fire at +14. A negative gap means audiences scored the film
higher. A buyer should notice the pattern. The two films with the weakest
reviews in the franchise are also the two where the audience disagreed most with
the critics. That is a warning against reading critic scores as a sign of
demand.

A scatter of `rt_critic_score` against `rt_audience_score` with a 45 degree
reference line, labelled per film. The page must carry the caveat that audience
scores were gathered over twenty five years while critic scores were fixed at
release. So the gap can be read, but it is not a like for like comparison.

### 4. Geography

**Title:** "Franchise search interest is nearly saturated across Western markets:
Canada ranks 9th of 61 countries at 97, within two points of the leaders."

The squeeze at the top of this ranking is partly caused by how Trends works,
because the index is scaled to the highest value within the request. So the
honest reading is that Canada is a top tier market, not that it is exactly
ninth. The page should say so.

A filled map from `dim_country`, with Canada highlighted through
`dim_country[is_canada]`. This dimension is unrelated to the date table, so the
page has no date slicer, and a text note says the data is a snapshot and not a
series.

### 5. Product line

**Title:** *Blocked.* Intended: "Price per piece on the branded line has risen
faster than inflation, which is the licensing premium a buyer pays."

A scatter of `Average Price Per Piece` by release year with a trend line and the
comparison adjusted for inflation. **I cannot finish this page** until I have a
Brickset key, because Rebrickable has no retail price. Piece counts, years,
themes and minifigure counts are all there, so I can build the page and it will
fill in as soon as the price source is collected.

### 6. Timing

**Title:** "The category peaks in December at 172 and collapses to 86 in January,
while franchise attention barely moves, so the premiere lands after the money has
been spent."

This is the page that carries my main argument. `Seasonality Index` by month for
the focus category and for total retail, with `Franchise Attention` laid over it
on a second axis, the premiere date marked, and the gift buying window shaded.
The matching static figure is
[`../images/figures/seasonality_attention_vs_retail.png`](../images/figures/seasonality_attention_vs_retail.png).

## Slicers

Two, on every page, which is what I planned.

- **Era** from `dim_date[era]`: `original` (2001 to 2011), `middle` (2012 to
  2022), `revival` (2023 to 2027). The values come from `eras` in `config.yaml`.
  If I change the boundaries there and rerun the star schema script, the slicer
  updates.
- **Country** from `dim_country[country_name]`. It affects the Geography page.
  That dimension is unrelated, so it cannot filter the other pages. The
  Geography page should say so on the page, so a reader does not have to find
  out that the slicer does nothing elsewhere.

Set both to sync across pages in the Sync Slicers pane.

## Rebuilding from scratch

1. Run `python src/analysis/23_star_schema.py`. It writes ten CSVs into
   `dashboard/model/`.
2. In Power BI Desktop: **Get Data, Text/CSV**, and load all ten.
3. In **Model view**, create the eight relationships from the table above.
   Power BI will detect some of them by itself, and it will guess wrong at least
   once, so check each cardinality and cross filter direction against the table.
4. Mark `dim_date` as a date table using `month_start`.
5. Create a blank table called `Measures`, and paste the DAX above into it.
6. Build the six pages.
7. Export each page to PNG and save it into `images/dashboard/`, then copy the
   figures used in the report into `images/figures/`.

Step 7 is the step that finishes my third goal for the dashboard. It is also the
only step here that needs a person with Power BI installed.
